raw_case_text:
We report the case of a 9-year-old male patient with a history of recurrent pulmonary infections and multiple operations to correct congenital heart defects (Figure 1). The patient was diagnosed with Fallot's Tetralogy at birth, and had a Blalock-Taussig surgery 3 days after birth, correction of pulmonary atresia at age 2 and correction of Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD), associated with enlargment of the right ventricle's outflow tract and insertion of an RV-PA conduit at age 4. Ten months after the last surgical intervention, the patient was admitted to the Emergency Department presenting with dyspnea and respiratory insufficiency, and was admitted due to suspicion of pneumonia. CT scan didn't show pulmonary involvement, but revealed dilation of the RV-PA conduit (Figure 2), and the patient was taken to surgery. Vegetations consistent with mycotic pseudoaneurysm were found in the outflow tract of the right ventricle, and the conduit was excised. Empirical antifungal treatment was started with micafungin for 4 days, with no clinical improvement, followed by fluconazole for 4 days. After this 8-day period, cultures from a sample of pleural fluid and of fragment of the conduit removed in surgery were positive for Trichosporon asahii. Both samples were cultured on Sabouraud dextrose agar and blood agar medium, but the time of positivity was not described, and susceptibility test was not performed for either samples. Species was identified using VITEK   identification system with specific cards for fungi and yeasts identification, but unfortunately no images of the colonies were taken. After this, Voriconazole was started and kept for 28 days and the patient responded well.
One month later, he presented with clinical deterioration, and a new CT scan showed images compatible with pulmonary necrosis in the upper segment of the right lower pulmonary lobe (Figure 3). The patient went under thoracotomy with segmentectomy of the middle lobe of the right lung. During the procedure, a pulmonary abscess was identified in the medium lobe. Biopsy showed the presence of septate hyphae with dichotomous branching, suggesting aspergillosis. After 17 days of admission, the patient was released with his usual drug regimen (Digoxin and Furosemide) along with Voriconazole for 30 days.
Four years later, at the age of 9, he was readmitted to our service presenting intermittent fever associated with nocturnal diaphoresis, dry cough, anxiety, anorexia and chest pain with a respiratory distress pattern. He was admitted for investigation, and a CT scan once again evidenced vegetation in the RV-PA conduit (Figure 4). Once more, cultures were positive for T. asahii, this time two blood samples cultured on Sabouraud and blood agar medium, which tested positive after 7 and 8 days, respectively. Again, VITEK  was used for identification and susceptibility testing was not performed. Antifungal treatment was once again started with Voriconazole and the patient was sent into surgery to exchange the RV-PA conduit. Voriconazole therapy was kept for two months. The drug was suspended when blood cultures were negative for T. asahii. The patient progressed well, with no other episodes of fever or other complaints.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 9-year-old boy with surgically repaired Tetralogy of Fallot and a right ventricle-to-pulmonary artery (RV-PA) conduit presented with recurrent episodes of dyspnea, respiratory insufficiency, intermittent fever, nocturnal diaphoresis, dry cough, and chest pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: At age 5 (10 months after RV-PA conduit insertion), the patient presented to the emergency department with dyspnea and respiratory insufficiency; CT revealed RV-PA conduit dilation and surgical excision confirmed a Trichosporon asahii mycotic pseudoaneurysm treated with voriconazole for 28 days. One month later, he clinically deteriorated with right lower/middle lobe necrosis and pulmonary abscess requiring segmentectomy, which revealed aspergillosis on biopsy. Four years later, at age 9, he was readmitted with intermittent fever, nocturnal diaphoresis, dry cough, anxiety, anorexia, and chest pain with respiratory distress.
subjective.past_medical_history: Tetralogy of Fallot with pulmonary atresia and VSD diagnosed at birth; underwent Blalock-Taussig shunt at 3 days of life, pulmonary atresia correction at age 2, and VSD repair with RV outflow tract enlargement and RV-PA conduit insertion at age 4; history of recurrent pulmonary infections. Home medications included digoxin and furosemide.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for dyspnea, respiratory distress, intermittent fever, nocturnal diaphoresis, dry cough, chest pain, anorexia, and anxiety.

objective.physical_examination: Presented with respiratory insufficiency during the initial episodes and a respiratory distress pattern at age 9.
objective.routine_investigations: During the first episode (age 5), pleural fluid and excised RV-PA conduit cultures on Sabouraud dextrose and blood agar grew Trichosporon asahii (identified by VITEK). During the third episode (age 9), two peripheral blood cultures grew T. asahii after 7 and 8 days of incubation.
objective.advanced_workup: During the first episode, chest CT showed RV-PA conduit dilation without pulmonary parenchymal involvement, and surgery confirmed right ventricular outflow tract vegetations/mycotic pseudoaneurysm. One month later, repeat chest CT showed pulmonary necrosis in the superior segment of the right lower lobe, and right thoracotomy with middle lobe segmentectomy identified a pulmonary abscess whose biopsy histopathology demonstrated dichotomously branching septate hyphae consistent with aspergillosis. At age 9, chest CT again demonstrated a vegetation in the RV-PA conduit.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Recurrent Trichosporon asahii mycotic pseudoaneurysm/endocarditis of the RV-PA conduit (at ages 5 and 9, confirmed by conduit tissue, pleural fluid, and blood cultures) complicated after the first conduit replacement by a right middle lobe pulmonary abscess caused by Aspergillus (confirmed by surgical biopsy showing dichotomously branching septate hyphae). The pulmonary aspergillosis abscess was successfully treated with right thoracotomy segmentectomy and 30 days of oral voriconazole alongside digoxin and furosemide, and the late recurrent T. asahii conduit infection at age 9 was cured with surgical RV-PA conduit exchange and 2 months of voriconazole therapy until blood cultures cleared.
